extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in political institutions and American democracy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting principles and evaluative standards for understanding the social and political institutions of the United States (township, county, State, inheritance law, suffrage, municipal freedom) as set out in Tocqueville's Democracy in America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Puritanical from English origins when judging Anglo-Americans
rubrics_metrics.description: To form a judgment on the Anglo-Americans of the present day it is necessary to distinguish what is of Puritanical and what is of English origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cautions against drawing too general or absolute inferences from the settlers’ influence alone, because emigrants mixed habits and notions from their education and traditions with new practices; when evaluating American institutions, carefully separate elements deriving from Puritan traditions versus those retained from English law and customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess criminal/civil procedure by its impact on the poor vs rich
rubrics_metrics.description: The civil and criminal procedure of the Americans has only two means of action—committal and bail...a legislation of this kind is hostile to the poor man, and favorable only to the rich.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate legal procedures by whether they require security (bail) that the poor cannot provide, thereby subjecting them to pretrial incarceration and distress while allowing the wealthy to avoid imprisonment and reduce penalties to fines. Use this as an index of aristocratic bias in law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin institutional analysis with a nation's social condition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Social condition is commonly the result of circumstances, sometimes of laws, oftener still of these two causes united; but wherever it exists, it may justly be considered as the source of almost all the laws, the usages, and the ideas which regulate the conduct of nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking to understand legislation and manners, start with the social condition (demography, customs, material circumstances) because it produces or modifies laws; do not analyze laws in isolation from underlying social structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate inheritance (law of descent) as a primary political institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of descent...ought nevertheless to be placed at the head of all political institutions; for, whilst political laws are only the symbol of a nation’s condition, they exercise an incredible influence upon its social state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how rules of succession (entail, primogeniture, partible inheritance) influence the concentration or dispersion of property and power across generations, and hence the strength of aristocratic vs democratic social structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge partible (equal) inheritance by its tendency to disperse landed property
rubrics_metrics.description: In virtue of the law of partible inheritance, the death of every proprietor brings about a kind of revolution in property...property, and especially landed property, must have a tendency to perpetual diminution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the legal regime of equal division to predict perpetual fragmentation of estates, the erosion of family-held landed wealth, and consequent weakening of landed aristocracy over generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider psychological/familial effects of inheritance laws on preservation of estates
rubrics_metrics.description: When the equal partition of property is established by law, the intimate connection is destroyed between family feeling and the preservation of the paternal estate...a man thinks of his present convenience; he provides for the establishment of his succeeding generation, and no more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate not just mechanical division of property but how inheritance rules change heirs' dispositions—whether family pride and intergenerational stewardship persist or decline, affecting willingness to keep estates intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess economic incentives created by fragmentation of estates
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong pecuniary interest in favor of selling, as floating capital produces higher interest than real property...Great landed estates which have once been divided never come together again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estates fragment, appraise market and yield incentives that encourage sale rather than re-consolidation (small proprietors cultivate more ardor, floating capital yields higher returns). These economic forces accelerate decline of large landed properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure degree of social cohesion by presence of established names and local authority
rubrics_metrics.description: In the new States of the West...the inhabitants are but of yesterday. Scarcely known to one another, the nearest neighbors are ignorant of each other’s history...society has no existence among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether communities have longstanding family names, local elites, shared history, and mutual knowledge; absence indicates 'society' is not fully formed and democracy is at an extreme without embedded social hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate educational equality and access as indicators of social leveling
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary instruction is within the reach of everybody; superior instruction is scarcely to be obtained by any...Most of the rich men were formerly poor; most of those who now enjoy leisure were absorbed in business during their youth...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how broadly primary versus higher education are available: broad primary schooling with limited higher education suggests a middle standard of knowledge, weak transmission of intellectual leisure across generations, and contributes to social equality of capacities and tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use presence/absence of aristocratic elements to gauge democratic predominance
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the aristocratic element has always been feeble from its birth...the democratic principle has gained so much strength by time, by events, and by legislation, as to have become not only predominant but all-powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a society, examine whether family or corporate authorities endure and whether individual character enjoys durable influence; weak aristocratic elements indicate a dominant democratic social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predict political outcomes from social equality (twofold risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the same social position, then, nations may derive one or the other of two great political results...the sovereignty of all and the absolute power of one man...there exists also...a depraved taste for equality, which impels the weak to attempt to lower the powerful to their own level, and reduces men to prefer equality in slavery to inequality with freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the level of social equality to anticipate political tendencies: either expansion of popular sovereignty or slide toward despotism through a perverted desire for enforced equality; evaluate society’s institutions and moral feelings to judge which path is likelier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess explicit institutionalization of the sovereignty of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the principle of the sovereignty of the people...is recognized by the customs and proclaimed by the laws; it spreads freely, and arrives without impediment at its most remote consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure how openly and practically the doctrine of popular sovereignty is embedded in laws, customs, electoral practices, and municipal life; its being explicit and practiced is a positive indicator of self-governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate extension of electoral franchise once qualifications are altered
rubrics_metrics.description: When a nation modifies the elective qualification, it may easily be foreseen that sooner or later that qualification will be entirely abolished...the further electoral rights are extended, the greater is the need of extending them; concession follows concession, and no stop can be made short of universal suffrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat changes that lower electoral qualifications as part of a cumulative process tending toward universal suffrage; use past concessions to forecast future democratizing reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological priority: study States (township, county, State) before the Federal Union
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to examine the State in order to possess a clue to the remainder...The Federal Government is...the exception; the Government of the States is the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyzing the U.S. political system, begin with the internal organization and functioning of townships, counties, and States rather than the federal structure, because State-level institutions are foundational and more representative of everyday governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vitality of municipal institutions (town-meetings) as measure of popular liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Town-meetings are to liberty what primary schools are to science; they bring it within the people’s reach, they teach men how to use and how to enjoy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess municipal independence and the existence of active town-meetings as essential indicators of a healthy democratic spirit; the robustness of local assemblies correlates with the strength and durability of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate durability of municipal freedom by its consolidation in law and public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: No immunities are so ill protected from the encroachments of the supreme power as those of municipal bodies...they cannot defend their cause with success unless it be identified with the customs of the nation and supported by public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Municipal liberties are fragile; judge their permanence by whether they are embedded in long-standing laws, national habits, and public opinion rather than mere administrative forms or transient privileges.
